html:
The Nuremberg trials were a series of trials of Nazi leaders held by the Allied powers in Nuremberg, Germany, after World War II. The first and best known, before the International Military Tribunal, ran from November 1945 to October 1946.

Judges from the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union tried 22 top figures of Nazi Germany. Twelve were sentenced to death, and Hermann Goering killed himself the night before his execution. Three were acquitted. The charges included crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, a new idea in law. "Following orders" was ruled no defence.

Twelve more trials of doctors, judges, industrialists and officers followed in American courts until 1949.

The trials set the base of modern international criminal law, and later courts drew on them. They also left gaps. Thousands of lower-ranking people were never tried, and men like Adolf Eichmann, who had planned the deportations, slipped away. His capture is told in the Mossad operation of 1960. The Allied push to punish and re-educate Germans soon faded in the denazification that followed, as the Cold War began.
